Food insecurity, and the distinction between chronic and transitory (acute) insecurity and famine
The central insight that hunger is usually a failure of access and distribution, not of total production (Amartya Sen's entitlement approach)
Industrial/globalized vs local/regional food systems, food miles, and food deserts

claims.claim: A food system encompasses the full farm-to-table chain: production, processing, distribution, retail, consumption, and loss/waste.

Per the 1996 World Food Summit definition used by the FAO, food security exists when all people, at all times, have physical, social, and economic access to sufficient, safe, and nutritious food that meets their dietary needs and food preferences for an active and healthy life.

The FAO frames food security through four dimensions: availability (food physically present via production, reserves, imports), access (resources/entitlements to obtain food), utilization (adequate diet, clean water, sanitation, and health to reach nutritional well-being), and stability (all three holding at all times).

Food insecurity can be chronic (persistent, poverty-linked) or transitory (short-term, shock-driven); severe short-term insecurity is termed acute, and famine is the extreme large-scale collapse of food access.

Amartya Sen's entitlement approach (Poverty and Famines, 1981) argues that starvation results from people's inability to establish command over food (entitlements via production, ownership, and exchange) rather than from a decline in aggregate food availability; the 1943 Bengal famine occurred without an aggregate food shortage.
The FAO's SOFI 2025 report estimated about 673 million people (8.2 percent of the world population, range 638-720 million) faced hunger in 2024, down from 8.5 percent in 2023 and 8.7 percent in 2022.
In 2024 hunger continued to rise in most subregions of Africa (above 20 percent, about 307 million people) and Western Asia (about 12.7 percent, more than 39 million people), per SOFI 2025.

A food desert is defined by the USDA as a low-income area with low access to affordable fresh food, operationally more than one mile from a supermarket in urban tracts and more than ten miles in rural tracts.

Food miles measure the distance food travels from producer to consumer; longer food miles are associated with more transport-related emissions, but transport is only one component of a food's total footprint, so local sourcing is not automatically lower-impact.

The FAO's 2011 study estimated that roughly one-third of food produced for human consumption, about 1.3 billion tonnes a year, is lost or wasted, with losses concentrated early in the chain in lower-income countries and consumer-level waste concentrated in higher-income countries.

conflictingEvidence.issue: The 2024 global hunger figure is a range with a midpoint, and different outlets emphasize different numbers.
positions: SOFI 2025 point estimate: about 673 million people / 8.2 percent for 2024
SOFI 2025 reported range: 638 to 720 million people
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson quotes the point estimate 'about 673 million (8.2 percent)' and also gives the 638-720 million range, always attributed to the FAO SOFI 2025 report (covering 2024) with the year stated.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Who coined the term 'food miles' is attributed differently across sources.
positions: Some sources credit UK activist Andrea Paxton (Lumen OER)
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson avoids naming a single originator and states only that the term was popularized in the 1990s, which both sources support.

unsupportedExistingClaims: The generated draft was machine boilerplate ('Food Systems is a foundational concept in Human Geography... a simple way to apply it') with no substantive, sourced claims about food security, supply chains, access, or deserts.
correctionsNeeded: Replaced the boilerplate entirely with the FAO food-security definition and four dimensions, the supply-chain stages, the access/entitlement insight, and food deserts/food miles.
Ensured every hunger/undernourishment figure carries a year and FAO SOFI 2025 attribution.
Kept farming/production content out of scope and explicitly handed it to the agriculture topic; named-and-handed-off economics/development and environment.
Attributed the access-not-supply argument to Amartya Sen and presented the Bengal famine factually as his analysis, not as an uncontested fact.
rightsIssues: FAO materials (concept note, SOFI 2025, food-loss study) are treated as REFERENCE_ONLY: facts and definitions synthesized into original prose; the 1996 food-security definition is a standard, widely reproduced treaty-style formulation quoted only as the established definition.
The VIVA Pressbooks Human Geography OER is CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 (non-commercial); treated as REFERENCE_ONLY, no wording reused, facts synthesized.
The Lumen/OpenStax 'Sustainability: A Comprehensive Foundation' chapter is CC BY 4.0; facts used with attribution, no wording reproduced.

fao.org hosts and the Pressbooks host returned HTTP 403 to the automated fetcher; the Pressbooks page and FAO SOFI figures were read via curl with a browser user-agent and via the FAO newsroom summary respectively, and figures were cross-checked across the FAO newsroom and UNICEF's SOFI 2025 posting. Notes on each record state which copy was actually read.

sourceRecords.title: An Introduction to the Basic Concepts of Food Security
sourceRecords.notes: Supports the 1996 World Food Summit definition of food security and the four dimensions: availability, access, utilization, stability; and the chronic vs transitory distinction. The PDF is binary and did not extract via the fetcher; the definition and four-dimension content were verified via web-search corroboration quoting this FAO document and cross-checked against the FAO SOFI 2023 online glossary (https://www.fao.org/3/cc3017en/online/state-food-security-and-nutrition-2023/annexes11.html), which states the same four dimensions and access-as-entitlements language. Facts synthesized; no wording reproduced beyond the standard definition.

sourceRecords.title: The State of Food Security and Nutrition in the World 2025 (SOFI 2025)
sourceRecords.notes: Released 28 July 2025. Supports: about 673 million people (8.2 percent of the world) faced hunger in 2024, within a 638-720 million range; down from 8.5 percent (2023) and 8.7 percent (2022); hunger rose in most of Africa (above 20 percent, ~307 million) and Western Asia (~12.7 percent, >39 million). fao.org blocked the fetcher (HTTP 403); figures read via the FAO newsroom summary (https://www.fao.org/newsroom/detail/global-hunger-declines--but-rises-in-africa-and-western-asia--un-report/en) and cross-checked against UNICEF's SOFI 2025 posting (https://data.unicef.org/resources/sofi-2025/). Report PDF mirror: https://data.unicef.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/08/SOFI-Report-2025.pdf

sourceRecords.title: Poverty and Famines: An Essay on Entitlement and Deprivation
sourceRecords.provider: Amartya Sen (Oxford University Press / Clarendon Press)
sourceRecords.notes: The 1981 monograph introducing the entitlement approach: starvation results from people's inability to establish command over food (entitlements via production, ownership, exchange) rather than from aggregate food-availability decline; the 1943 Bengal famine analyzed as a case where food was available but particular groups' entitlements collapsed. Verified via the Harvard Scholars publication page and web-search corroboration summarizing the book's argument. Attributed as Sen's argument. No wording reproduced.

sourceRecords.title: Introduction to Human Geography (VIVA Pressbooks) - Agricultural & Food Systems
sourceRecords.notes: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 (non-commercial, so treated as reference-only). Read via curl with a browser user-agent (the plain fetcher was blocked/HTTP 403). Supports: food security as 'steady, affordable, and safe access to sufficient food' and food insecurity as its opposite; food deserts with the USDA parameters (urban 1+ mile, rural 10+ miles, low-income); the point that food-desert status and food insecurity are not identical (access depends on physical, social, financial capability); famine defined as large-scale hunger; and the attribution to Amartya Sen that famines are failures of the system linking food supply to demand (Bengal 1943, price inflation, poor distribution, hoarding). Facts synthesized; no wording reproduced.

sourceRecords.title: Sustainability: A Comprehensive Foundation - Food Miles
sourceRecords.provider: Lumen Learning / OpenStax CNX (Theis and Tomkin)
sourceRecords.notes: CC BY 4.0. Read via WebFetch 2026-08-19. Supports: food miles as 'the distance food travels from producer to consumer,' popularized in the 1990s; a globalized food system spanning continents in a single meal, lowering some transport costs while raising emissions and reducing local-economy support; the case for local food systems (freshness, less processing, local economies, resilience). Used to support the supply-chain framing and the food-miles limitation. Facts synthesized into original prose; no wording reproduced.

sourceRecords.title: Global Food Losses and Food Waste - Extent, Causes and Prevention
sourceRecords.notes: FAO-commissioned 2011 study. Supports: roughly one-third of food produced for human consumption (~1.3 billion tonnes/year) is lost or wasted; food losses (production, harvest, post-harvest, processing) dominate in developing countries due to infrastructure and technology gaps, while consumer-level food waste dominates in industrialized countries. fao.org blocked the fetcher; figures verified via the UN News summary (https://news.un.org/en/story/2011/05/374722) and the FAO newsroom summary of the same study. No wording reproduced.
